Longitudinal pipe buckling Failure can also occur from buckling not of the cross section but of the length of pipe between supports. Pipes that are buried generally will not suffer from this failure mode since the soil provides continuous support (we neglect cases where buckling is possible due to erosion under the pipe). In 10 these buckling cases, the driving force is the dynamic pressure on the pipe due to effective wind load from the blast, loading the pipe along its length. Failure occurs when the pipe material goes entirely into plastic deformation across the cross section, creating a plastic hinge that continues to deform with no additional loading (hardening of the pipe material is neglected). The internal pressure in the pipe has a negligible effect in longitudinal buckling, since it provides hoop stress in the pipe but not necessarily longitudinal stresses. The pipe is assumed to have a 0.7 coefficient of drag. A key factor in this calculation is estimating the distance between supports in an arbitrary pipe network.
